syllabusOutcomes.13.1: Understand and use vector notation in any form: column vectors, AB with an arrow, bold p, ai − bj. Correct notation is expected
syllabusOutcomes.13.2: Know and use position vectors and unit vectors (the unit vector in the direction of a is a/|a|)
syllabusOutcomes.13.3: Find the magnitude of a vector; add and subtract vectors and multiply by scalars; equate like vectors; solve vector-geometry problems
syllabusOutcomes.13.4: Compose and resolve velocities; find a resultant; use a velocity vector to find position and solve problems in context such as particles colliding

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Given that \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix}-3\\7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(4\overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\end{pmatrix}\), find \(\overrightarrow{RQ}\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The vectors a, b and c are such that \(\mathbf{a} = \alpha\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}\), \(\mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i}+\beta\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{c} = (2\alpha+5\beta)\mathbf{i}+20\mathbf{j}\). Given that \(\mathbf{c} = 3\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}\), find the values of α and β.

questions.statement:
(a) Given that \(\;\overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix}-3\\7\end{pmatrix}\;\) and \(\;4\overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\end{pmatrix}\), find \(\overrightarrow{RQ}\). [2]

(b) The vectors \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\) are such that \(\;\mathbf{a} = \alpha\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}\), \(\;\mathbf{b} = 4\mathbf{i}+\beta\mathbf{j}\;\) and \(\;\mathbf{c} = (2\alpha+5\beta)\mathbf{i}+20\mathbf{j}\), where α and β are scalars.

Given that \(\;\mathbf{c} = 3\mathbf{a}-2\mathbf{b}\), find the values of α and β. [3]
tips: (a) Careful — you are given \(4\overrightarrow{PR}\), not \(\overrightarrow{PR}\). Divide by 4 FIRST: \(\overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}-0.5\\2\end{pmatrix}\).
(a) Route rule: \(\overrightarrow{RQ} = \overrightarrow{RP} + \overrightarrow{PQ} = -\overrightarrow{PR} + \overrightarrow{PQ}\). Reversing an arrow flips the sign.
(b) Equate like components — the i's with the i's and the j's with the j's. That gives two equations in α and β.
The j-equation \(20 = 18 - 2\beta\) has only β in it — solve that one first, then substitute.
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}-2.5\\5\end{pmatrix}\) oe (B1 for \(-\frac14\begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}-3\\7\end{pmatrix}\) oe soi)
(b) M1 — equates like vectors at least once: \(3\alpha - 8 = 2\alpha+5\beta\) or \(18-2\beta = 20\)
(b) A2 — \(\alpha = 3\), \(\beta = -1\) (A1 for either value correct)

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A particle P moves with a speed of 14.5 parallel to the vector \(\begin{pmatrix}-20\\21\end{pmatrix}\). Find the velocity vector of P.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Initially, P has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Write down the position vector of P at time t.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: A second particle Q has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}-5\\7.5\end{pmatrix}t\) at time t. Find, in terms of t, the distance between P and Q at time t. Simplify your answer.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Hence show that P and Q never collide.

questions.statement:
In this question, all distances are in metres and time, \(t\), is in seconds.

A particle \(P\) moves with a speed of 14.5 parallel to the vector \(\begin{pmatrix}-20\\21\end{pmatrix}\).

(a) Find the velocity vector of \(P\). [2]

Initially, \(P\) has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

(b) Write down the position vector of \(P\) at time \(t\). [2]

A second particle \(Q\) has position vector \(\;\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}-5\\7.5\end{pmatrix}t\;\) at time \(t\).

(c) Find, in terms of \(t\), the distance between \(P\) and \(Q\) at time \(t\). Simplify your answer. [4]

(d) Hence show that \(P\) and \(Q\) never collide. [2]
tips: (a) Velocity = speed × unit vector. Find \(\left|\begin{pmatrix}-20\\21\end{pmatrix}\right| = \sqrt{400+441} = 29\) (a 20-21-29 triple), then multiply the direction by \(\tfrac{14.5}{29} = \tfrac12\).
(b) Position at time t = start + velocity × t. Write it as a single column vector or as \(\mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{v}t\).

(c) The vector between them is \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \mathbf{r}_Q - \mathbf{r}_P\); the distance is its magnitude \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Expand and collect under the root — do NOT try to simplify \(\sqrt{\ }\) further.

(d) Collision means distance = 0. Set the quadratic inside the root to zero and show its discriminant is negative — so no real \(t\) exists. (Discriminant \(= -1936\).) A negative discriminant is the whole argument.
solution: Discriminant \(= (-28)^2 - 4(34)(20) = 784 - 2720 = -1936 < 0\): no real roots, so there is no time at which the distance is zero — they never collide. ✓
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}-10\\10.5\end{pmatrix}\) or \(\frac12\begin{pmatrix}-20\\21\end{pmatrix}\) (B1 for \(\left|\begin{pmatrix}-20\\21\end{pmatrix}\right| = 29\) soi, or one correct element)
(b) 2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-10\\10.5\end{pmatrix}t\) oe (M1 FT on their velocity vector)
(c) 2 — \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix}5t-4\\-3t-2\end{pmatrix}\) oe (dep M1 on M1 in (b)); M1 dep — \(PQ = \sqrt{(5t-4)^2+(-3t-2)^2}\); A1 — \(\sqrt{34t^2-28t+20}\)
(d) M1 — for collision \(34t^2-28t+20 = 0\) soi (using their quadratic from (c)); A1 — discriminant \(= -1936\), so no real roots so no collision oe

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: A particle P is moving in a straight line with a speed of 26 in the direction of the vector \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Find the velocity vector of P.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: When t = 0, P passes through a point A which has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Write down the position vector of P at time t.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: At the same time that P passes through A, a particle Q passes through a point B. The position vector of Q at time t is \(\begin{pmatrix}8t-5\\2-25t\end{pmatrix}\). The distance between P and Q at time t is d. Show that \(d^2 = mt^2+nt+r\), where m, n and r are integers to be found.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Hence show that P and Q do not collide.

questions.statement:
In this question lengths are in centimetres and time, \(t\), is in seconds.

A particle \(P\) is moving in a straight line with a speed of 26 in the direction of the vector \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-12\end{pmatrix}\).

(a) Find the velocity vector of \(P\). [2]

When \(t=0\), \(P\) passes through a point \(A\) which has position vector \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix}\).

(b) Write down the position vector of \(P\) at time \(t\). [2]

At the same time that \(P\) passes through \(A\), a particle \(Q\) passes through a point \(B\). The position vector of \(Q\) at time \(t\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}8t-5\\2-25t\end{pmatrix}\). The distance between \(P\) and \(Q\) at time \(t\) is \(d\).

(c) Show that \(\;d^2 = mt^2+nt+r\), where \(m\), \(n\) and \(r\) are integers to be found. [3]

(d) Hence show that \(P\) and \(Q\) do not collide. [1]
tips: (a) \(\left|\begin{pmatrix}5\\-12\end{pmatrix}\right| = 13\) (the 5-12-13 triple). Scale factor \(\tfrac{26}{13} = 2\), so velocity \(= \begin{pmatrix}10\\-24\end{pmatrix}\).
(c) Subtract the position vectors (either order — squaring removes the sign), then use \(d^2 = x^2+y^2\). Here \(d^2\) is asked for, so no square root is needed at all.
(d) This one factorises: \(d^2 = 5t^2+40t+80 = 5(t+4)^2\). So \(d = 0\) only when \(t = -4\).
The killer argument: time cannot be negative (\(t \geqslant 0\)), so \(d\) is never zero in the real motion — they do not collide. Say this explicitly.
solution: (d) \(d = 0 \Rightarrow 5t^2+40t+80 = 5(t+4)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow t = -4\). But \(t \geqslant 0\), so this never happens: \(P\) and \(Q\) do not collide. ✓
markScheme: (a) 2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-24\end{pmatrix}\) oe isw (B1 for the magnitude of the direction vector = 13 soi, or M1 for \(\sqrt{5^2+(-12)^2}\))
(b) 2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}10\\-24\end{pmatrix}\) oe isw (M1 FT their velocity vector)

(c) B1 — the difference of the two position vectors, e.g. \(\begin{pmatrix}8+2t\\4+t\end{pmatrix}\) oe soi; M1 — finds \(d^2\) or \(d\) from it (FT their (b)); A1 — \(d^2 = 5t^2+40t+80\) (mark final answer)
(d) B1 dep on (c) correct — a correct argument including d, e.g. when \(d=0\), \(t=-4\) but \(t\geqslant0\) [so no collision]

topics: resolving a speed at an angle

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Particle A starts from the origin O at time t = 0. It moves with constant speed 10 ms⁻¹ in the direction 60° above the x-axis. Find the exact values of the components of the velocity of particle A in the x-direction and the y-direction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find, in terms of t, the position vector of particle A at time t.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Particle B starts from the point \((2\sqrt3, 9)\) at time t = 0. It moves with constant speed \(\tfrac53\) ms⁻¹ parallel to the positive x-axis. Find, in terms of t, the position vector of particle B at time t.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Hence show that the particles collide.

questions.statement:
In this question \(\mathbf{i}\) is a unit vector in the positive \(x\)-direction and \(\mathbf{j}\) is a unit vector in the positive \(y\)-direction. Time is in seconds and distances are in metres.

Particle \(A\) starts from the origin \(O\) at time \(t=0\). It moves with constant speed 10 ms⁻¹ in the direction 60° above the \(x\)-axis.

(a) Find the exact values of the components of the velocity of particle \(A\) in the \(x\)-direction and the \(y\)-direction. [2]

(b) Find, in terms of \(t\), the position vector of particle \(A\) at time \(t\). [1]

Particle \(B\) starts from the point \((2\sqrt3, 9)\) at time \(t=0\). It moves with constant speed \(\dfrac53\) ms⁻¹ parallel to the positive \(x\)-axis.

(c) Find, in terms of \(t\), the position vector of particle \(B\) at time \(t\). [2]

(d) Hence show that the particles collide. [4]
tips: (a) Resolving: a speed \(v\) at angle θ to the x-axis has components \(v\cos\theta\) (horizontal) and \(v\sin\theta\) (vertical).
(a) "Exact values" → use the special angles: \(\cos60° = \tfrac12\) and \(\sin60° = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), giving 5 and \(5\sqrt3\). No decimals.
(c) "Parallel to the positive x-axis" means the y-component of the velocity is ZERO — B moves horizontally only, so its \(y\) stays 9.

(d) Collision = both coordinates match at the SAME time. Set the \(y\)'s equal to find \(t\), then check that this same \(t\) also makes the \(x\)'s equal. Finding one \(t\) is not enough — the second check is where the marks are.
solution: The two times are identical, so both coordinates agree at \(t = \dfrac{3\sqrt3}{5}\) — the particles collide (at the point \(\left(3\sqrt3, 9\right)\)). ✓
markScheme: (a) B2 — \(x = 5\), \(y = 5\sqrt3\) (B1 for either component correct)
(b) B1 — \(\left[\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\right] t\begin{pmatrix}5\\5\sqrt3\end{pmatrix}\) oe isw (FT their velocity, which must have at least one non-zero component)
(c) B2 — \(\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt3\\9\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}\frac53\\0\end{pmatrix}\) oe isw (B1 for the x-component \(2\sqrt3+\frac53t\) or the y-component 9 seen)
(d) M1 — \(5t\sqrt3 = 9\) or \(5t = 2\sqrt3+\frac53t\) (FT their position vectors, both in terms of t); A1 — both equations stated correctly

(d) A2 — shows the exact times are the same, e.g. \(t = \frac{9}{5\sqrt3} = \frac{3\sqrt3}{5}\) AND \(\frac{10}{3}t = 2\sqrt3 \to t = \frac{3\sqrt3}{5}\) (A1 for one correct value of t; alternatively find t and show it satisfies the other equation, or show both particles are at \(\left(\frac{9}{\sqrt3}, 9\right)\))

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Point P has position vector 2i + 5j relative to an origin O. At 1300, boat A sails from point P with velocity vector 8i + 8j. Find the position vector of A at the end of 2 hours of sailing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Write down the position vector of A at the end of t hours of sailing.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Point Q has position vector 20i + 8j relative to the origin O. At 1500, boat B sails from point Q on a bearing of 300° with a constant speed of 5√3. Find the position vector of B at 1700.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find the distance between the two boats at 1700.

questions.statement:
In this question, \(\mathbf{i}\) is a unit vector due east and \(\mathbf{j}\) is a unit vector due north. Distances are measured in kilometres and time is measured in hours.

Point \(P\) has position vector \(2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}\) relative to an origin \(O\).
At 13 00, boat \(A\) sails from point \(P\) with velocity vector \(8\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}\).

(a) Find the position vector of \(A\) at the end of 2 hours of sailing. [1]

(b) Write down the position vector of \(A\) at the end of \(t\) hours of sailing. [1]

(c) Point \(Q\) has position vector \(20\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}\) relative to the origin \(O\). At 15 00, boat \(B\) sails from point \(Q\) on a bearing of 300° with a constant speed of \(5\sqrt3\).

Find the position vector of \(B\) at 17 00. [3]

(d) Find the distance between the two boats at 17 00. [3]
tips: Track the clock carefully: A sails from 1300, so at 1700 it has sailed 4 hours. B sails from 1500, so at 1700 it has sailed only 2 hours. Mismatched times are the number-one error here.
(c) Bearings are measured clockwise from NORTH, so with i = east and j = north: \(v_x = v\sin(\text{bearing})\), \(v_y = v\cos(\text{bearing})\).

(c) Bearing 300°: \(\sin300° = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\cos300° = \tfrac12\). So velocity \(= 5\sqrt3\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\mathbf{i} + 5\sqrt3\left(\tfrac12\right)\mathbf{j} = -7.5\mathbf{i} + \tfrac{5\sqrt3}{2}\mathbf{j}\) — north-west, which matches a bearing of 300°. Sanity-check the signs against the compass.
(d) Distance = magnitude of the difference of the two 1700 position vectors.
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(18\mathbf{i}+21\mathbf{j}\) oe isw (allow unsimplified \(2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+2(8\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})\))
(b) B1 — \(2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+t(8\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})\) oe isw

(c) B3 — \(5\mathbf{i}+(8+5\sqrt3)\mathbf{j}\) oe isw (B2 for both velocity components \(x=-7.5\), \(y=\frac{5\sqrt3}{2}\) or 4.33[01…] soi; B1 for each correct component; SC1 for reversed components)
(d) 3 — 35.4[21…] (marks for a correct distance calculation using their 1700 position vectors)

position vector of a point on a segment

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The position vectors of A and B relative to an origin O are \(\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\6\end{pmatrix}\). The point C lies on AB with AC : CB = 3 : 1. The point D lies on OA such that \(\overrightarrow{OD}=\lambda\overrightarrow{OA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{CD}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\-5.5\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{OD}\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Hence find the value of λ.

questions.statement:
The position vectors of points \(A\) and \(B\) relative to an origin \(O\) are

\(\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix}-4\\6\end{pmatrix}\).

The point \(C\) lies on \(AB\) and is such that \(AC : CB = 3 : 1\).

The point \(D\) lies on \(OA\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{OD} = \lambda\overrightarrow{OA}\;\) and \(\;\overrightarrow{CD} = \begin{pmatrix}5\\-5.5\end{pmatrix}\).

(a) Find \(\overrightarrow{OD}\). [5]

(b) Hence find the value of \(\lambda\). [1]
tips: Ratio on a line: \(AC:CB = 3:1\) means \(\overrightarrow{AC} = \tfrac34\overrightarrow{AB}\) — the 3 is out of a total of 4 parts, not out of 1.
\(\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix}-8\\8\end{pmatrix}\), so \(\overrightarrow{OC} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \tfrac34\overrightarrow{AB}\).
Then walk the route: \(\overrightarrow{OD} = \overrightarrow{OC} + \overrightarrow{CD}\).
(b) \(\overrightarrow{OD} = \lambda\overrightarrow{OA}\): compare either component — \(3 = 4\lambda\) gives \(\lambda = 0.75\). Check the other component agrees (\(-1.5 = 0.75\times-2\) ✓).
markScheme: (a) B1 — \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix}-8\\8\end{pmatrix}\) oe soi (allow component vectors throughout)

(a) 2 — \(\overrightarrow{OC} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\) (M1 for \(\overrightarrow{OC} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\frac34\overrightarrow{AB}\) oe, or \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\6\end{pmatrix}-\frac14\overrightarrow{AB}\))
(a) 2 — \(\overrightarrow{OD} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-1.5\end{pmatrix}\) (M1FT for \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-5.5\end{pmatrix}+\)their \(\overrightarrow{OC}\); mark final answer, must be a vector)
(b) B1 — \(\lambda = 0.75\) or \(\frac34\) (must have full marks in part (a))

topics: equating coefficients of a and b

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The diagram shows triangle OAB where OA = a and OB = b. P lies on OA with \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OA}\); Q lies on AB with \(\overrightarrow{AQ}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}\). The line through P and Q meets the line through O and B at R, where \(\overrightarrow{OR}=\lambda\mathbf{b}\) and \(\overrightarrow{PR}=\mu\overrightarrow{PQ}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{OR}\) in terms of a, b and μ.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Hence find the values of λ and μ.

questions.statement:
The diagram shows the triangle \(OAB\), where \(\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}\).

The point \(P\) lies on \(OA\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{OP} = \tfrac34\overrightarrow{OA}\).
The point \(Q\) lies on \(AB\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{AQ} = \tfrac13\overrightarrow{AB}\).

The straight line through \(P\) and \(Q\) meets the straight line through \(O\) and \(B\) at the point \(R\). It is given that \(\;\overrightarrow{OR} = \lambda\mathbf{b}\;\) and \(\;\overrightarrow{PR} = \mu\overrightarrow{PQ}\), where λ and μ are constants.

(a) Find \(\overrightarrow{OR}\) in terms of \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mu\). [6]

(b) Hence find the values of \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\). [3]
tips: Route-building is the whole method: express everything in terms of \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) by walking along the arrows.
\(\overrightarrow{OQ} = \mathbf{a} + \tfrac13(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) = \tfrac23\mathbf{a}+\tfrac13\mathbf{b}\), and \(\overrightarrow{OP} = \tfrac34\mathbf{a}\).
\(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP} = \tfrac13\mathbf{b} - \tfrac{1}{12}\mathbf{a}\). Then \(\overrightarrow{OR} = \overrightarrow{OP} + \mu\overrightarrow{PQ}\).

(b) \(R\) is on \(OB\), so \(\overrightarrow{OR}\) has no \(\mathbf{a}\) component: set the coefficient of \(\mathbf{a}\) to zero to get μ, then read λ off the \(\mathbf{b}\) coefficient. This 'coefficient must be zero' step is the exam's favourite idea.
markScheme: (a) 2 — \(\overrightarrow{OQ} = \mathbf{a}+\frac13(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})\) oe (M1 for an attempt \(\overrightarrow{OQ} = \mathbf{a}+k(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})\), k any sign; allow unsimplified)
(a) M1 — \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = -\frac34\mathbf{a} + their\ \overrightarrow{OQ}\); A1 — \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \frac13\mathbf{b}-\frac{1}{12}\mathbf{a}\) (allow unsimplified)
(a) B1 — \(\overrightarrow{OP} = \frac34\mathbf{a}\) (allow anywhere); B1 — \(\overrightarrow{OR} = \frac34\mathbf{a}+\mu\left(\frac13\mathbf{b}-\frac{1}{12}\mathbf{a}\right)\) oe, must be simplified
(b) B1 — \(\lambda = \frac13\mu\) (equating b vectors); B1 — \(\frac34-\frac{1}{12}\mu = 0\) oe (equating a vectors to zero); B1 — \(\mu = 9\), \(\lambda = 3\)

questions.statement:
A triangle \(OAB\) is such that \(\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}\).

The point \(X\) lies on \(OA\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{OA} = 3\overrightarrow{OX}\).
The point \(Y\) lies on \(XB\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{XB} = 5\overrightarrow{XY}\).
The point \(Z\) lies on \(OB\) such that \(\;\overrightarrow{OB} = m\overrightarrow{OZ}\), where \(m\) is a scalar.
\(\overrightarrow{OX} = n\overrightarrow{ZY}\), where \(n\) is a scalar.

Use a vector method to find the values of \(m\) and \(n\). [8]
tips: Read each condition the right way round: \(\overrightarrow{OA}=3\overrightarrow{OX}\) means \(\overrightarrow{OX} = \tfrac13\mathbf{a}\) (X is a THIRD of the way, not three times).

Likewise \(\overrightarrow{XB}=5\overrightarrow{XY}\Rightarrow \overrightarrow{XY}=\tfrac15\overrightarrow{XB}\), and \(\overrightarrow{OB}=m\overrightarrow{OZ}\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OZ}=\tfrac1m\mathbf{b}\).

Build \(\overrightarrow{ZY}\) by a route: \(\overrightarrow{ZY} = \overrightarrow{ZO}+\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XY} = -\tfrac1m\mathbf{b} + \tfrac13\mathbf{a} + \tfrac15\left(\mathbf{b}-\tfrac13\mathbf{a}\right)\).

Then \(\overrightarrow{OX} = n\overrightarrow{ZY}\) gives TWO equations by comparing \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) coefficients. The \(\mathbf{b}\) one has no left-hand side, so it equals zero — that gives \(m\).
markScheme: B1 — \(\overrightarrow{OX} = \frac13\mathbf{a}\) (allow on a diagram if the direction is clear)
B1 — \(\overrightarrow{XB} = \mathbf{b}-\frac13\mathbf{a}\);  B1 — \(\overrightarrow{XY} = \frac15\left(\mathbf{b}-\frac13\mathbf{a}\right)\) oe
B1 — \(\overrightarrow{OZ} = \frac1m\mathbf{b}\) (do not accept \(m\overrightarrow{OZ}=\mathbf{b}\) unless recovered)

M1 — \(\overrightarrow{ZY} = -\frac1m\mathbf{b}+\frac13\mathbf{a}+\frac15\left(\mathbf{b}-\frac13\mathbf{a}\right)\) oe, in a and b (FT their \(-\overrightarrow{OZ}+\overrightarrow{OX}+\overrightarrow{XY}\))
M1 dep — uses \(\frac13\mathbf{a}\) equated to their \(n\overrightarrow{ZY}\) oe
A2 — \(m = 5\), \(n = \frac54\) (A1 for each)
